title: Provide primary emergency care/first aid as an advanced first responder

lessons.title: Scene safety, assessment and calling for help
lessons.html:
Your role as a first responder

On a farm or yard, help can be far away. A trained first responder keeps a casualty alive and stable until emergency services arrive. Typical incidents include kicks and falls from horses, tractor accidents, chemical splashes, snakebite, heat illness and cuts. This lesson gives knowledge only. You must complete practical training with an accredited first aid provider before acting as a first aider. The OHS Act 85 of 1993 requires employers to have trained first aiders and first aid boxes in many workplaces.

Step 1: Danger

Protect yourself first. Check for loose horses, running machinery, electricity, traffic, fire, chemicals and aggressive animals. Make the scene safe or wait for help. Wear disposable gloves to protect against blood-borne infections such as HIV and hepatitis B.

Step 2: Response

Speak loudly and tap the shoulders: "Can you hear me?" Note the level of response using AVPU: Alert, responds to Voice, responds to Pain, Unresponsive.

Step 3: Call for help

Shout for help and have someone phone emergency services: 10177 for an ambulance, or 112 from a cell phone. Give the exact location (farm name, GPS pin, directions from the main road), what happened, the number of casualties and their condition. Send someone to the gate to guide the ambulance.

Step 4: Airway and breathing

Open the airway with a head tilt, chin lift (use a jaw thrust if spinal injury is suspected and you are trained). Look, listen and feel for normal breathing for up to 10 seconds. Occasional gasps are not normal breathing.

Step 5: Circulation and severe bleeding

Look for and control severe bleeding at once.

Secondary survey

When life threats are managed, check from head to toe for injuries, take a history (what happened, medical conditions, medicines, allergies) and monitor vital signs. Write down the times and findings to hand over to paramedics.

lessons.title: CPR, bleeding and shock
lessons.html:
Cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR)

If an adult is unresponsive and not breathing normally:

  1. Make sure emergency services have been called and ask for an AED (defibrillator) if one is available.
  2. Kneel beside the casualty, place the heel of one hand in the centre of the chest, the other hand on top.
  3. Press down about 5 to 6 cm, at a rate of 100 to 120 compressions a minute. Let the chest rise fully between compressions.
  4. After 30 compressions, give 2 rescue breaths if you are trained and willing, using a face shield or pocket mask.
  5. Continue 30:2 without stopping until the casualty starts breathing normally, help takes over, or you are too exhausted to continue.
  6. Switch on the AED as soon as it arrives and follow its voice prompts.

Recovery position

An unresponsive casualty who is breathing normally, with no suspected spinal injury, is placed on their side in the recovery position to keep the airway open. Keep checking breathing.

Severe bleeding

  • Apply firm, direct pressure on the wound with a sterile dressing or clean cloth.
  • If blood soaks through, add more pads on top and keep pressing.
  • Bandage firmly but not so tight that fingers or toes turn blue.
  • Lay the casualty down. For life-threatening limb bleeding that direct pressure cannot stop, a tourniquet may be used by those trained in it; note the time it was applied.
  • Do not remove an embedded object; pad around it.

Shock

Shock is a dangerous drop in blood flow to the organs, often from blood loss, burns or severe allergic reactions. Signs: pale, cold, sweaty skin; fast, weak pulse; fast breathing; thirst; confusion.

  • Treat the cause, such as bleeding.
  • Lay the casualty down and keep them warm.
  • Do not give food or drink.
  • Reassure and monitor breathing and response until help arrives.

lessons.title: Injuries and medical emergencies on the farm
lessons.html:
Head and spinal injuries

Falls from horses and kicks often cause head and spinal injuries. If a casualty fell from height, was kicked in the head or neck, or has neck pain, numbness or tingling, suspect a spinal injury. Keep the head and neck still in line with the body. Do not move the casualty unless there is immediate danger. Do not remove a riding helmet unless it is essential to open the airway and you are trained to do so.

Fractures and dislocations

  • Signs: pain, swelling, deformity, inability to use the limb.
  • Support the limb in the position found, using padding, slings or splints.
  • Check circulation beyond the injury.
  • For open fractures, cover the wound with a sterile dressing; do not push bone back.

Burns

Cool the burn under cool running water for at least 20 minutes. Remove rings and watches before swelling. Cover loosely with cling film or a clean, non-fluffy dressing. Do not apply butter, toothpaste or ointments. Do not burst blisters. Severe or large burns need hospital care.

Chemical exposure

Remove contaminated clothing and rinse skin or eyes with plenty of clean water for at least 15 to 20 minutes. Take the product label or safety data sheet to the hospital.

Snakebite

Keep the casualty calm and still, remove rings and tight items, and get them to hospital urgently. Do not cut, suck, apply ice or use a tourniquet. For neurotoxic bites (such as from mambas or cobras) a pressure bandage may be recommended by your training provider. If venom is spat into the eyes, rinse with plenty of water.

Heat illness

Move the casualty to shade, loosen clothing, cool with water and fanning, and give sips of water if fully conscious. Confusion or collapse indicates heatstroke: call 10177 immediately.

Other medical emergencies

  • Seizures: protect from injury, do not restrain or put anything in the mouth, recovery position afterwards.
  • Diabetic emergency: if conscious and able to swallow, give a sugary drink.
  • Severe allergic reaction: help the person use their own adrenaline auto-injector; call for help.

Key points

  • Danger, Response, call for help, Airway, Breathing, Circulation.
  • Phone 10177 or 112 and send someone to guide the ambulance.
  • CPR: 30 compressions to 2 breaths, 5 to 6 cm deep, 100 to 120 per minute.
  • Control severe bleeding with firm direct pressure.
  • Keep suspected spinal injuries still; cool burns for 20 minutes.
  • Practical training by an accredited provider is required.
